paper.title: Modified Poisson-Nernst-Planck Model with Coulomb and Hard-sphere Correlations

context: The paper delivers a 1D two-plate mPNP model with two energetic corrections: a WKB-based generalized Debye-Huckel Coulomb self-energy (Eq. 3.22) and a MFMT hard-sphere functional with six weighted densities (Eqs. 2.26-2.30), on a uniform finite-difference grid over the accessible region |x| <= 1-a, with Robin BCs at the Stern layer. The following five questions were surfaced by the replication process itself and are genuinely open (not answered by the paper as written and not answered by the replication in report/REPORT.md).

open_questions.q: Would an adaptive mesh (radially refined near the Stern-layer boundary at x = +/-(1-a)) substantially reduce the number of grid points needed to reach a given error target, versus the uniform grid used in the paper (h ~ 4.25e-3 at N=401)?
open_questions.basis: The paper reports second-order convergence of the MFMT chemical potential on a uniform mesh (Fig. 4.1(b)), and the replication confirms observed order 2.000 over N in {200,400,800,1600,3200}. But the physically interesting behaviour -- SC cation peak at x=-0.850 with c_+^max = 2.0943 (18.7% larger than MF), and the whole diffuse-layer structure -- is concentrated within an a-thick boundary layer, while the interior is nearly flat. This is a textbook adaptive-mesh regime, yet the paper uses only uniform grids and neither the paper nor the replication tests whether an r-adaptive or hp-adaptive scheme retains the 2nd-order rate while cutting cost.
open_questions.next_steps: (1) Add an equidistribution-based adaptive 1D grid concentrating nodes in [-(1-a), -(1-a)+3a] and mirror; (2) rerun the MFMT convergence test at matched degrees-of-freedom N_adaptive vs N_uniform and report the effective order and prefactor; (3) rerun the SC nested Newton at N_adaptive = 100, 200, 400 and check convergence to the N=401 uniform values for c_+^max and Q_left; (4) confirm the endpoint linear-interpolation correction still yields O(h^2) on non-uniform meshes.

open_questions.q: How does the 1D two-plate mPNP model extend to realistic 3D biomolecular geometries (nanopore, ion channel, DNA/protein surface), and does the WKB Coulomb self-energy of Eq. 3.22 remain quantitatively useful once curvature and multi-body dielectric structure enter?
open_questions.basis: The paper is explicitly 1D (parallel slabs, symmetric 1:1 electrolyte, L in [2,12] nm) and the WKB derivation of Eq. 3.22 uses the slab geometry to yield the dielectric-mismatch parameter gamma = (1 - eta_b)/(1 + eta_b). The replication touches only 1D MF and SC. Whether the same MFMT + Coulomb-correlation structure survives in a 3D cylindrical nanopore or on a Poisson-Boltzmann grid around a DNA fragment is not settled by either the paper or the replication.
open_questions.next_steps: (1) Formulate the generalized Debye-Huckel Green function in a cylindrical channel with axisymmetric dielectric profile epsilon(r,z) and derive (or numerically compute) the diagonal Green function G(r,r); (2) implement MFMT in cylindrical coordinates with the correct weighted-density kernels (n_3 becomes a spherical convolution truncated by the channel wall); (3) benchmark against a 3D nanopore case with published all-atom MD (e.g. alpha-hemolysin at 1 M KCl) and check whether the LS sub-model retains its 5% MC-agreement claim from Fig. 4.3(a) in this curved geometry.

open_questions.q: Can the MFMT + Coulomb-correlation LS free-energy be systematically improved by coupling to MD-derived ion-pair or triplet correlation functions g_ij(r), rather than relying on the mean-spherical / GDH closure implicit in Eq. 3.22?
open_questions.basis: The paper's SC piece is MFMT (a functional of one-body density only), and the LC piece is a Gaussian-fluctuation (WKB) estimate around the mean field. Neither ingests measured pair correlations. The paper compares to MC and MD data (C5-C7) but the model does not learn from them. The replication similarly treats the MFMT as fixed. A hybrid closure that uses MD g_ij(r) at bulk conditions to constrain a bridge functional B[c_i] added to Eq. 2.27 could plausibly improve the LS-vs-MD gap at c_0 = 90 mM and L = 5 nm (Fig. 4.3(c)), but is untested.
open_questions.next_steps: (1) Extract g_++(r), g_+-(r), g_--(r) from a well-equilibrated 1:1 electrolyte MD trajectory at c_0 = 100 mM; (2) fit a Percus-Yevick-corrected bridge function B[c_i] whose functional derivative reproduces the pair-correlation-implied second-order direct correlation function c^(2)(r) at bulk; (3) plug B into the mPNP free energy and re-solve the SC and LS steady problems; (4) compare c_+(x) profiles against the raw MD histogram in the same slab and quantify whether the improvement is worth the added closure complexity.

open_questions.q: Do higher-order finite-volume or discontinuous-Galerkin schemes give measurable robustness or accuracy gains over the paper's finite-difference discretisation (Eqs. 3.23-3.31) in stiff regimes (large gamma, high surface charge, small L)?
open_questions.basis: The paper uses centred finite differences with Robin BCs (Eq. 3.14) and reports 2nd-order accuracy in Fig. 4.1(b). The replication's Newton solver hits |R| = 3.5e-12 (MF) and residual mu_rel_diff = 8.7e-10 (SC) at the moderate parameters (epsilon,q,a,V)=(0.2,0.3,0.15,1). Neither addresses regimes where the paper flags numerical difficulty -- large dielectric mismatch (gamma near 1) with strong surface charge (0.02 C/m^2) and small L (~2 nm), where the Stern-layer boundary layer collapses. Whether a flux-limited finite-volume or a p=3 DG scheme survives these regimes with fewer iterations or without spurious oscillations is not tested.
open_questions.next_steps: (1) Implement a 1D finite-volume scheme with harmonic-mean face fluxes for the mPNP steady problem; (2) implement a p=2 nodal DG scheme on the same grid; (3) stress-test all three (FD/FV/DG) at (gamma, V, L) in {(0.95, 2, 0.5), (0.99, 3, 0.3)} in dimensionless units; (4) compare iteration counts to a fixed residual, presence of spurious oscillations in phi'(x) near the Stern layer, and eventual peak c_+^max within 1% of a reference N=6401 FD solution.

open_questions.q: How does the mPNP-LS model compare against a density-functional-theory-Poisson-Boltzmann (DFT-PB) or classical DFT solver for electrolyte transport, on a common benchmark of ion selectivity and rectification in a nanopore under an applied potential?
open_questions.basis: The paper positions itself against the classical mean-field PB and validates the equilibrium density profiles against MC/MD (C5-C7). It does not compare against a full classical-DFT solver (e.g. one that uses MFMT for hard-sphere plus the Mean-Spherical Approximation for electrostatics), and it does not benchmark transport observables (current, rectification ratio, selectivity coefficient) under bias. The replication also only tests equilibrium (steady) densities. Whether mPNP-LS gives the same or better transport predictions than a competing DFT-PB scheme at matched cost is an open question relevant to whether practitioners should adopt mPNP as a workhorse.
open_questions.next_steps: (1) Fix a common benchmark: 1:1 electrolyte at c_bulk = 100 mM in a cylindrical channel with radius 1 nm, length 5 nm, applied bias 100 mV, dielectric mismatch gamma = 0.95; (2) implement mPNP-LS (requires the WKB self-energy piece deferred in this replication) and a competing MFMT-plus-MSA classical-DFT-PNP with the same MFMT kernel; (3) compare steady-state I-V, cation-vs-anion selectivity, and computational cost; (4) if practical, verify against a reference all-atom MD nonequilibrium simulation of the same system to break ties.
